title: WHY DID GOD CHOOSE RAHAB?
paragraphs: WHY DID GOD CHOOSE RAHAB?
There are names in Scripture that seem to belong in the shadows.
Names we expect God to overlook.
Names that make us uncomfortable because they remind us too much of ourselves.
Rahab is one of those names.
When most people hear her story, they remember a single detail.
She was a prostitute.
The Bible does not hide it.
It does not soften it.
It does not attempt to rewrite her past.
Instead, Scripture repeatedly reminds us of it.
"Rahab the prostitute."
Again and again.
As if God wanted future generations to see something extraordinary.
Not the scandal.
The grace.
Because if God could redeem Rahab, then nobody is beyond redemption.
The story begins in the city of Jericho.

Ancient Jericho stood directly in the path of Israel's conquest of the Promised Land. It was a fortified city overflowing with idolatry, pagan worship, moral corruption, and resistance against the God of Israel.
Rahab lived there.
She was not raised among God's covenant people.
She was not an Israelite.
She did not grow up hearing the Torah.
She had no religious pedigree.
No spiritual résumé.
No respected family lineage.
No obvious qualifications.
Yet when God looked upon Jericho, He saw a woman whose heart was already moving toward Him.
And that changes everything.
The Hebrew text introduces her as אִשָּׁה זוֹנָה (ishah zonah)—a woman who practiced prostitution (Joshua 2:1).
Many readers stop there.
God does not.
Because while humanity often defines people by their worst chapter, God sees the entire story He intends to write.
The spies arrived secretly in Jericho.
The king heard about it immediately.
A search began.
Anyone helping Israel would be considered a traitor.
The safest thing Rahab could have done was betray the spies.
The logical thing.
The profitable thing.
The self-preserving thing.
Instead, she hid them.
Risking her reputation.
Risking her future.
Risking her life.
Why?
The answer is found in one of the most remarkable confessions of faith in the entire Old Testament.
She told the spies:
"I know that the LORD has given you the land..." (Joshua 2:9).
Notice those words.
Not "I think."
Not "I wonder."
Not "I hope."
"I know."
The divine name used in the Hebrew text is יהוה (YHWH), often rendered LORD in English translations.
Rahab was surrounded by pagan gods.
Yet she recognized the true God.
She continued:
"For the LORD your God, He is God in heaven above and on earth beneath." (Joshua 2:11)
This is astonishing.
Many Israelites struggled to believe that.
Yet a Gentile woman living in a pagan city proclaimed the sovereignty of God.
The Hebrew declaration is powerful:

יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵיכֶם הוּא אֱלֹהִים
(YHWH Eloheikhem Hu Elohim)
"The LORD your God, He is God."
This was not merely intellectual agreement.
This was surrender.
Faith.
Trust.
A heart turning toward God.
The New Testament confirms this understanding.
Hebrews 11 places Rahab among the heroes of faith.
Think about that for a moment.
The chapter contains names like Abel, Noah, Abraham, Moses, and David.
And there, among giants of faith, stands Rahab.
Not because of her past.
Because of her faith.
Hebrews 11:31 says:
"By faith Rahab the prostitute did not perish with those who were disobedient."
By faith.
Not by performance.
Not by moral perfection.
Not by religious credentials.
Faith.
The Greek word used here is πίστις (pistis).
It means trust, confidence, reliance upon.
Rahab entrusted herself to the God she had come to know.
Faith transformed everything.
But there is something even more beautiful.
God did not merely spare Rahab.
He adopted her into His story.
Matthew's genealogy contains a detail that many readers overlook.
Rahab became the mother of Boaz.
Boaz became the father of Obed.
Obed became the father of Jesse.
Jesse became the father of David.
And generations later, from that same family line, came Jesus Christ.
The Messiah.
The Savior of the world.
Rahab did not simply survive judgment.
She became part of redemption history.
Imagine the scandal.
Imagine the whispers.
Imagine the conversations.
"Do you know who she used to be?"
"Do you know where she came from?"
"Do you know what she did?"
Yet every accusation was overwhelmed by grace.
Because God was writing a larger story.
A story pointing toward Jesus.
This is one of the central themes of Scripture.
God delights in rescuing the unlikely.
Abraham was old.
Jacob was a deceiver.
Moses was a fugitive.
David was a shepherd.
Peter was impulsive.
Paul persecuted Christians.
Rahab was a prostitute.
The pattern is unmistakable.
God's grace is greater than human failure.
Not because sin is small.
But because Christ is great.
The Gospel does not teach that our past does not matter.
The Gospel teaches that Jesus matters more.
When Jesus entered the world, He came for people exactly like Rahab.
Broken people.
Ashamed people.
Wounded people.
People carrying secrets.
People convinced they could never be used by God.
People who assume their story has already been written.
Then Jesus arrives.
And everything changes.
The Greek word often translated "grace" is χάρις (charis).
It carries the idea of undeserved favor.
A gift.
Something freely given.
Rahab's story is grace in action.
She did not earn her place in God's family.
She received it.
The scarlet cord hanging from her window has long been viewed by many Christians as a beautiful picture pointing forward to salvation through Christ.
The same God who spared Rahab through faith now offers salvation through the blood of Jesus.
The same God who welcomed Rahab welcomes sinners today.
The same God who rewrote her story still rewrites stories.
Maybe that is why Rahab's account continues to grip hearts thousands of years later.
Because deep down, we all know what it feels like to carry regret.
To wonder if our failures are too great.
To fear that our mistakes have become our identity.
Rahab reminds us that God's grace reaches further than our shame.
Further than our past.
Further than our worst decisions.
The cross stands as eternal proof.
When Jesus cried, "It is finished" (John 19:30), the Greek word was τετέλεσται (tetelestai).
Paid in full.
Completed.
Accomplished.
The debt of sin was settled.
For Rahab.
For Peter.
For Paul.
For you.
For me.
And perhaps that is the real question.
Not why God chose Rahab.
But why God continues choosing people like us.
The answer is found in the heart of the Gospel.
Because Jesus came to seek and save the lost.
Because grace is greater than scandal.
Because redemption is stronger than shame.
Because no story surrendered to Christ remains the same.
Someone in your circle may need this reminder today.
Testimonies of God's grace strengthen believers and point others toward Christ.

The devil wanted Rahab remembered for her shame. God chose to remember her for His grace.
